book.author: Stephen R. Jordan
book.volume: Volume X of The Operating Discipline for AI Library

name: Preschool Through Second Grade

title: Preschool Through Second Grade
answer: In a 2026 study, researchers asked 310 children aged 4 to 6 where they would go to learn how something in science works. The children could choose a digital voice assistant, a classmate, or their classroom teacher.

papers.why: Young children may trust AI over teachers; adults must model checking.
papers.title: How Do Children Evaluate Scientific Explanations Provided by Digital Voice Assistants, Teachers, and Peers?
papers.finding: Children aged 4-6 (N=310) preferred to ask and trust a voice assistant over a peer or even a classroom teacher for science explanations.

papers.why: PreK adoption hinges on teacher confidence and peer norms.
papers.title: Exploring factors influencing preschool teachers’ behavioral intention to use AI technologies in early childhood settings
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Survey of 270 preschool teachers (TAM): AI self-efficacy was the strongest driver of intention to use AI, followed by subjective norm and perceived usefulness.

papers.why: Ready model for PreK AI literacy built with teachers.
papers.title: Play with AI (PL-AI): A play-centered, design-based curriculum for AI literacy in pre-K and kindergarten
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Design-based research, four teachers, descriptive only.
papers.finding: Play with AI (PL-AI): seven play-based activities for pre-K and kindergarten co-designed with four teachers: unplugged how-to algorithms, Bee-Bot and Ozobot coding, and dialogue with a social robot comparing story endings. Teacher confidence and ownership grew; evidence is qualitative and formative, not validated learning gains.

papers.why: First PreK home-literacy GenAI evidence: useful supplement, not a substitute for a parent or teacher.
papers.title: Conversational AI in children's home literacy learning: effectiveness, advantages, challenges, and family perception
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: LLM voice tutor (Vovo) for vocabulary and story co-construction, 10 families, children aged 3-7, six weeks, 150 sessions. Delivered structured literacy as consistently as parents, but children learned more with parents. Strengths: consistency, language modeling, verbal encouragement. Weaknesses: speech recognition, persistence, nonverbal cues, phonemes. Children preferred parents for emotional bonding.

papers.title: Children’s selective trust in technological informants: A meta-analysis.
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 20 studies (ages 3-10): no overall preference for tech vs human informants; older children trust technology more; more trust in search tools than conversational agents.

papers.why: Children trust chatbots readily; design and lessons must build checking habits.
papers.title: Ask Me Anything: Exploring Children’s Attitudes Toward an Age-tailored AI-powered Chatbot
papers.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
papers.finding: 63 students ages 6-14 used a topic-limited child chatbot: high trust, anthropomorphizing; some tested it with known answers.

papers.title: Utilization of AI-aided vocabulary teaching in K-12: A case study
papers.finding: Grade 1 EFL, 20 per group, 10 weeks: AI-generated picture cards beat paper cards on post-tests, but the advantage vanished on a delayed test.

papers.title: Error-preserving Automatic Speech Recognition of Young English Learners' Language
papers.finding: Standard speech recognition trained on adult native speech transfers poorly to children learning English and smooths over their errors, so it cannot give accurate correction without child-specific tuning.

papers.why: Privacy literacy gap in primary grades.
papers.title: "Alexa doesn't have that many feelings": Children's understanding of AI through interactions with smart speakers in their homes
papers.finding: Scottish children aged 6-11: most overestimated smart speakers' intelligence, were unsure about feelings, and lacked understanding of data privacy.

papers.why: Young children already treat voice assistants as fact sources.
papers.title: Children’s trust in and learning from voice assistants.
papers.finding: Ages 4-5 and 7-8: with age, children trusted voice assistants more for facts and humans more for personal information.

papers.why: Gives the book a one-sentence AI idea suitable for PreK-2 and an equity argument for teaching it early.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence education for young children: Why, what, and how in curriculum design and implementation
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: ECE position report on why, what, and how of AI for young children. Core idea children can explore: AI learns patterns from lots of data to predict and recommend. Treats AI literacy as part of digital literacy and raises digital equity.

papers.why: Robots are mostly studied with young children in short trials.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence-based robots in education: A systematic review of selected SSCI publications
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Review of SSCI studies on AI robots in education: most target learners under 13, run under 4 weeks, in language and science.

papers.why: Evidence base for the PreK chapter is small but positive.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in early childhood education: A scoping review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: Few studies, mostly proof-of-concept, short duration.
papers.finding: Scoping review of 17 ECE AI studies (1995-2021). Most reported gains in AI, machine learning, computing, and robotics concepts plus creativity, emotion control, collaborative inquiry, literacy, and computational thinking.

papers.why: Rare concrete PreK AI curriculum; confirms that very young children can learn simple AI ideas through play with a robot.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in early childhood education: Curriculum design and future directions
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: Design paper with limited evaluation; Hong Kong context.
papers.finding: Proposes a kindergarten (K3-5) AI curriculum framework: AI knowledge, AI skills, AI attitude, with four modules, five activities, and one project. A social robot used as learning companion and programmable artifact helped young children grasp AI ideas. Recommends problem-based learning.

papers.why: One of the few PreK studies in the library; supports adaptive practice for early concepts.
papers.title: Modelling and exploiting taxonomic knowledge for developing mobile learning systems to enhance children's structural and functional categorization
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Small quasi-experiment; screen time for young children needs limits.
papers.finding: Mobile app for preschoolers (ages 3-6) generated dynamic categorization examples from a knowledge model. Quasi-experiment: children using it scored higher on categorization than peers taught with books and worksheets.

papers.title: Your Child Missed Learning the Alphabet Today: A Randomized Trial of Sending Teacher-Written Postcards Home to Reduce Absences
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, 5,552 PreK to grade 2 students: postcards with a teacher note on missed content cut absences 8.3%.

papers.title: Using behavioral insights to increase attendance at subsidized preschool programs: The Show Up to Grow Up intervention
papers.venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in Chicago subsidized preschools: parent texts cut chronic absence 9.3 percentage points (20%).

children.name: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
children.blurb: In the early grades, most general AI tools are not made for young children, and several require adult educator accounts or parental consent before a student can be invited.

children.name: Speech and Early Reading
children.blurb: Speech technology is the most promising and most delicate AI tool for early reading, because it can listen to a child read, give feedback on missed words, and flag children who may need help.

children.name: Stories Made for One Classroom
children.blurb: Teachers can use approved AI tools to create decodable stories and small custom activities that match the exact letter sounds, sight words and themes their class is learning.

children.name: Routines, Schedules, and Social Stories
children.blurb: Routines, schedules, and social stories are visual and written supports that help young children, especially those with autism or anxiety, know what comes next and handle new experiences.

children.name: Observation and Family Communication
children.blurb: Observation and family communication in early childhood means using approved tools to turn a teacher's quick daily notes into organized records matched to early learning standards, and then into weekly family digests and conference talking points.

children.name: Teaching Young Children About Machines
children.blurb: Young children in preschool through second grade can begin learning how machines work through play based activities that need no screens, such as giving step by step instructions to a classmate acting as a robot or sorting pictures into groups.

children.name: Planning Play, Stations, and Circle Time
children.blurb: AI tools can quickly generate many small planning options for early childhood teachers, such as circle time questions, transition songs, and fine motor stations.

children.name: Behavior Notes Without Cameras
children.blurb: Behavior Notes Without Cameras is a way for early childhood teachers to spot patterns in a child's behavior using their own short written observations, organized with the help of an approved AI tool once names are removed, instead of camera based tracking.

children.name: Guardrails for the Youngest Learners
children.blurb: For preschool through second grade, the book sets three firm guardrails: no facial recognition or camera based tracking of young children, no stored voice recordings unless a family agrees and there is a clear reason, and child mode turned on for every device young children use.

children.name: For Parents: What a Tool Should Never Collect
children.blurb: Parents of young children should ask any AI tool used at school what it collects, how long it keeps it, whether it records voice or face, and whether the child's information improves company products.

children.name: Handing Off to Kindergarten
children.blurb: Handing off to kindergarten means using AI to help preschool teachers write short, careful profiles of each child so kindergarten teachers begin the year already knowing their strengths, interests, goals, and what helps them feel settled.

sections.body: This section covers the years before formal schooling through second grade, where the book says AI belongs mostly in the teacher's hands rather than the child's. The book opens with a study in which children aged 4 to 6 preferred to ask a digital voice assistant about science and trusted it over a classmate and even their teacher, and with a review of 20 studies finding that young children do not automatically prefer technology but that trust in it grows with age and is strongest for search tools. Because children this young cannot check what a machine tells them, the adults around them have to do that checking. The chapter then walks through the places where AI helps most in these grades, from speech and early reading to stories, routines, observation, family communication, and first lessons about how machines work, and it names the adult responsible for each idea.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book's rule for this grade band is that most AI use sits with the teacher, who uses it to plan, prepare, and communicate with families, and that when children do interact with AI an adult is present, the tool is set up for young users, and the goal is to learn about machines rather than from them. What works includes teacher facing uses such as decodable stories and weekly family digests, and the research it holds shows promise for play based AI literacy activities, teacher written notes home, and parent texts that cut absences. What does not work is a helpful app that quietly collects too much, asking for photos, voice recordings, or family details that were never needed while nobody reads the fine print. The book also notes that standard speech recognition transfers poorly to young children learning English and smooths over their errors, and that a vendor's privacy page is not enough on its own, since what counts is a district record checked against the guardrails and the never collect list.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move in the order the book lays out, starting with who uses AI in the early grades and then speech and early reading, where a teacher would go for the tools that support decoding and oral language. Stories made for one classroom and routines, schedules, and social stories show how a teacher can prepare material for a specific group, while observation and family communication and behavior notes without cameras cover the record keeping side of the room. Teaching young children about machines and planning play, stations, and circle time are the pages a teacher turns to when children do meet AI, since the goal there is learning about machines rather than from them. Guardrails for the youngest learners and the parent page on what a tool should never collect are where a leader or parent checks a tool against the never collect list, and handing off to kindergarten closes the section by showing how good notes help a child start strong.
sections.heading: How these pages fit together
